Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up clustering approach that produces a hierarchy by merging clusters upward. It begins with every object as its own singleton cluster and repeatedly merges the two most similar or closest clusters until either a single all-encompassing cluster remains or a specific stopping rule is reached.

The specific definition of cluster similarity used to decide which clusters to merge depends on the algorithm. Some techniques use the closeness of clusters, such as the single link method which measures the minimum distance between points in different clusters. Other algorithms, such as group average, base similarity on the strength of connections, such as the pairwise similarity of points between two clusters. Additionally, strategies may involve choosing clusters with the closest centroids or merging clusters that result in the smallest increase in total SSE (as seen in Ward's method).

For single-linkage agglomerative clustering, the distance between two clusters is defined by the formula:

$$ d_{single}(C_i, C_j) = \min_{x \in C_i, y \in C_j} d(x, y) $$

Agglomerative techniques are not suitable for very large data sets. Furthermore, because the process only merges and never separates objects, it can compound errors if objects are wrongly put together during the partitioning process.

candidate_system_evidence.text: CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives) is a clustering algorithm that uses a variety of different techniques to create an approach that can handle large data sets, outliers, and clusters with non-spherical shapes and non-uniform sizes. CURE represents a cluster by using multiple representative points from the cluster. These points will, in theory, capture the geometry and shape of the cluster. The first representative point is chosen to be the point farthest from the center of the cluster, while the remaining points are chosen so that they are farthest from all the previously chosen points. In this way, the representative points are naturally relatively well distributed. The number of points chosen is a parameter, but it was found that a value of 10 or more worked well. Once the representative points are chosen, they are shrunk toward the center by a factor, α . This helps moderate the effect of outliers, which are usually farther away from the center and thus, are shrunk more. For example, a representative point that was a distance of 10 units from the center would move by 3 units (for ), while a representative point at a distance of 1 unit would only move 0.3 units. CURE uses an agglomerative hierarchical scheme to perform the actual clustering. The distance between two clusters is the minimum distance between any two representative points (after they are shrunk toward their respective centers). While this scheme is not exactly like any other hierarchical scheme that we have seen, it is equivalent to centroid-based hierarchical clustering if , and roughly the same as single link hierarchical clustering if . Notice that while a hierarchical clustering scheme is used, the goal of CURE is to find a given number of clusters as specified by the user. CURE takes advantage of certain characteristics of the hierarchical clustering process to eliminate outliers at two different points in the clustering process. First, if a cluster is growing slowly, then it may consist of outliers, since by definition, outliers are far from others and will not be merged with other points very often. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering techniques operate by merging the two most similar clusters, where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm. Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity. candidate_draft: Agglomerative (Bottom-Up) Clustering is a hierarchical clustering method that starts with each data point as its own cluster and iteratively merges the closest clusters until a single cluster remains or a stopping criterion is met. This bottom-up approach contrasts with divisive clustering, which starts with a single cluster and splits it into smaller clusters. The merging process is guided by linkage criteria, such as single linkage, which considers the minimum distance between points in different clusters, or complete linkage, which considers the maximum distance. Agglomerative clustering is particularly useful for exploring the hierarchical structure of data and is often visualized using a dendrogram. expert_reference: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that produces a hierarchical clustering by starting with each point as a singleton cluster and repeatedly merging the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is a collection of closely related techniques where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm used. Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity. The single-linkage distance is defined as the minimum distance between any point in one cluster and any point in the other: d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y). Other merging strategies include the centroid method, which merges the clusters with the closest centroids, and Ward's method, which is a greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective to merge the two clusters that result in the smallest increase in total SSE. Agglomerative clustering is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward; in contrast, agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward. A key limitation of agglomerative hierarchical clustering is that it can never separate objects that have been wrongly put together, meaning it will only compound errors if the initial partitioning or merging decisions are incorrect. Additionally, if the data is very large, an agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique cannot be directly applied, often necessitating the use of divisive techniques or other methods like BIRCH that do not require all data to be in main memory.

candidate_draft: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method within the broader category of hierarchical clustering, which builds a nested hierarchy of clusters typically visualized as a dendrogram. The core procedure starts with every data point as its own singleton cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach requires defining a notion of cluster proximity to determine which pair of clusters is closest at each step. Unlike divisive hierarchical clustering, which is a top-down method that starts with one all-inclusive cluster and repeatedly splits it, agglomerative clustering builds the hierarchy by successive merging. Agglomerative techniques are by far the most common form of hierarchical clustering and are widely used because they are easy to define, do not require choosing the number of clusters (k) in advance, and can accommodate different distance metrics and linkage criteria. The method is greedy, meaning that once a merge is made, it cannot be undone, which can be problematic for noisy or high-dimensional data. It is also sensitive to the choice of linkage and feature scaling, and computing pairwise distances can be expensive for large datasets. The basic algorithm involves computing a proximity matrix and then iteratively merging the closest pair of clusters. The computational complexity is O(m^2) for the proximity matrix computation and O(m^2) for the merging iterations, where m is the number of data points. Agglomerative clustering is often preferred when the application requires a hierarchy, such as in taxonomy creation, and some studies suggest it can produce better-quality clusters than other methods. It avoids the difficulty of solving a hard combinatorial optimization problem by making local decisions at each step rather than globally optimizing an objective function.

expert_reference: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that produces a hierarchical clustering by starting with each point as a singleton cluster and repeatedly merging the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is a collection of closely related techniques where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm used. Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity. The single-linkage distance is defined as the minimum distance between any point in one cluster and any point in the other: d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y). Other merging strategies include the centroid method, which merges the clusters with the closest centroids, and Ward's method, which is a greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective to merge the two clusters that result in the smallest increase in total SSE. Agglomerative clustering is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward; in contrast, agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward. A key limitation of agglomerative hierarchical clustering is that it can never separate objects that have been wrongly put together, meaning it will only compound errors if the initial partitioning or merging decisions are incorrect. Additionally, if the data is very large, an agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique cannot be directly applied, often necessitating the use of divisive techniques or other methods like BIRCH that do not require all data to be in main memory.

candidate_draft: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that starts with every object as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until one large cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is a collection of closely related clustering techniques that produce a hierarchical clustering; some have a natural interpretation in terms of graph-based clustering, while others have an interpretation in terms of a prototype-based approach. The process is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward, whereas agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward. A key component of this method is the linkage criterion, which determines how the distance between two clusters is calculated. For example, single linkage defines the distance between two clusters as the minimum distance between any two points in the clusters, expressed as d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y), where C_i and C_j are the two clusters and d(x, y) is the distance between points x and y. Other linkage methods include complete linkage (farthest pair), average linkage (all cross-pairs), centroid linkage (centers), and Ward's method, which is described as greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective. The choice of linkage method is critical because using only one approach can lead to mistakes in merging clusters; for instance, using closeness (single link) might merge clusters that almost touch instead of clusters that are intuitively more similar based on connection strength. Agglomerative clustering is often selected for global clustering tasks because it can be applied to summary information stored in clustering features. However, it has limitations: if the data is very large, it may not be directly applicable, and it can compound errors if objects are wrongly put together in a prior partitioning step, as it can never separate objects that have been merged.

candidate_system_evidence.text: CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives) is a clustering algorithm that uses a variety of different techniques to create an approach that can handle large data sets, outliers, and clusters with non-spherical shapes and non-uniform sizes. CURE represents a cluster by using multiple representative points from the cluster. These points will, in theory, capture the geometry and shape of the cluster. The first representative point is chosen to be the point farthest from the center of the cluster, while the remaining points are chosen so that they are farthest from all the previously chosen points. In this way, the representative points are naturally relatively well distributed. The number of points chosen is a parameter, but it was found that a value of 10 or more worked well. Once the representative points are chosen, they are shrunk toward the center by a factor, α . This helps moderate the effect of outliers, which are usually farther away from the center and thus, are shrunk more. CURE uses an agglomerative hierarchical scheme to perform the actual clustering. expert_reference: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism. Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available. One specific divisive hierarchical technique is the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering. Divisive clustering is often considered when data is very large and agglomerative techniques cannot be directly applied, though the MST algorithm only works if the data set is not too large. Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, but it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory. In such large-scale situations, a technique such as BIRCH, which does not require that all data be in main memory, becomes more useful. The choice of clustering algorithm is often determined by the need to create a hierarchical clustering that extends only to the point of splitting data into a few hundred clusters rather than a complete hierarchy to individual objects.

candidate_draft: Divisive (top-down) clustering is a hierarchical clustering approach that builds a nested hierarchy of clusters by starting with a single, all-inclusive cluster containing all objects and repeatedly splitting clusters into smaller subclusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This contrasts with agglomerative (bottom-up) clustering, which starts with every object as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters. A complete specification of a divisive method must address three key questions: which cluster should be split, how that cluster should be split, and when the splitting should stop. The result of divisive clustering is typically displayed using a dendrogram, a tree-like diagram that shows the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which the clusters were split. Divisive clustering is useful for taxonomies and broad-to-specific segmentation, particularly when the top-level split is meaningful or when a good splitter is available. Specific divisive techniques include bisecting K-means and minimum spanning tree (MST) clustering, where the MST approach starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph. While agglomerative hierarchical clustering is by far the most common approach, divisive approaches have also received attention, with early work in taxonomy and later developments including Principal Direction Divisive Partitioning. Both divisive and agglomerative approaches typically treat merging or splitting decisions as final, though some work has attempted to overcome these limitations.

expert_reference: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism. Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available. One specific divisive hierarchical technique is the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering. Divisive clustering is often considered when data is very large and agglomerative techniques cannot be directly applied, though the MST algorithm only works if the data set is not too large. Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, but it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory. In such large-scale situations, a technique such as BIRCH, which does not require that all data be in main memory, becomes more useful. The choice of clustering algorithm is often determined by the need to create a hierarchical clustering that extends only to the point of splitting data into a few hundred clusters rather than a complete hierarchy to individual objects.

expert_reference: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism. Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available. One specific divisive hierarchical technique is the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering. Divisive clustering is often considered when data is very large and agglomerative techniques cannot be directly applied, though the MST algorithm only works if the data set is not too large. Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, but it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory. In such large-scale situations, a technique such as BIRCH, which does not require that all data be in main memory, becomes more useful. The choice of clustering algorithm is often determined by the need to create a hierarchical clustering that extends only to the point of splitting data into a few hundred clusters rather than a complete hierarchy to individual objects.

candidate_draft: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that operates by splitting clusters downward. It is one of two basic approaches for generating a hierarchical clustering, the other being agglomerative (bottom-up) clustering, which merges clusters. In divisive clustering, the process involves repeatedly splitting clusters, and the result depends strongly on the definition of the cluster split. A complete divisive clustering method requires a splitting rule to determine how the chosen cluster should be divided. This approach is useful when the top-level split is meaningful or when a good splitter is available. Specific examples of divisive hierarchical techniques include DIANA, a standard method found in the R cluster package, and MST, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph. Another technique, PDDP, is based on finding the first principal direction of the data. The resulting hierarchical structure is often displayed graphically using a dendrogram, which shows the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which the clusters were split.

expert_reference: Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by producing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits. Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points. The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2. This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. A key characteristic of this approach is that it makes local split decisions, meaning it does not jointly optimize all centroids at once; consequently, it can produce different results than standard K-Means with the same target number of clusters. The algorithm is often used to speed up clustering by reducing the number of similarity computations, as it only calculates distances for a subset of points to two centroids at each step rather than all points to all centroids. It is also noted for being less susceptible to initialization problems because it can perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). If a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from Bisecting K-Means can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step, although Bisecting K-Means itself is a valid standalone algorithm.

candidate_draft: Bisecting K-Means is a divisive-style clustering method and a straightforward extension of the basic K-means algorithm. It starts with the entire set of points and repeatedly bisects an existing cluster using ordinary K-means with k = 2 until the desired number of clusters is obtained. This process creates a hierarchical sequence of binary splits. By recording the sequence of clusterings produced as clusters are bisected, the method can also be used to produce a hierarchical clustering. Bisecting K-Means is noted as a scalable algorithm and is less susceptible to initialization problems than standard K-means. It is a valid algorithm in its own right, though it may be refined with standard K-means in some contexts. The method is distinct from standard K-means, which is a partitional clustering algorithm, and from other divisive or density-based approaches like DBSCAN.

expert_reference: Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by producing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits. Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points. The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2. This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. A key characteristic of this approach is that it makes local split decisions, meaning it does not jointly optimize all centroids at once; consequently, it can produce different results than standard K-Means with the same target number of clusters. The algorithm is often used to speed up clustering by reducing the number of similarity computations, as it only calculates distances for a subset of points to two centroids at each step rather than all points to all centroids. It is also noted for being less susceptible to initialization problems because it can perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). If a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from Bisecting K-Means can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step, although Bisecting K-Means itself is a valid standalone algorithm.

candidate_draft: Bisecting K-Means is a divisive-style clustering method and a straightforward extension of the basic K-Means algorithm. It starts with a single cluster containing all points and repeatedly splits one selected cluster into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2 until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. To obtain K clusters, the process requires K - 1 bisections; for example, to get 3 leaf clusters, the algorithm first splits all points into two clusters and then chooses one of those clusters to split again. The algorithm maintains a list of clusters, initially containing the cluster of all points. In each iteration, it removes a cluster from the list, performs several trial bisections of that chosen cluster using basic K-Means, and selects the two resulting clusters with the lowest total Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). These two clusters are then added back to the list. The process repeats until the list contains K clusters. Bisecting K-Means is less susceptible to initialization problems than standard K-Means because it performs multiple trial bisections and chooses the one with the lowest SSE, and because only two centroids are involved at each step. It is also a scalable algorithm that reduces the number of similarity computations by only computing distances for the subset of points in the cluster being bisected, rather than all points. By recording the sequence of clusterings produced as clusters are bisected, Bisecting K-Means can also be used to produce a hierarchical clustering. The resulting clusters are often refined by using their centroids as initial centroids for the standard K-Means algorithm.

expert_reference: Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by producing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits. Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points. The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2. This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. A key characteristic of this approach is that it makes local split decisions, meaning it does not jointly optimize all centroids at once; consequently, it can produce different results than standard K-Means with the same target number of clusters. The algorithm is often used to speed up clustering by reducing the number of similarity computations, as it only calculates distances for a subset of points to two centroids at each step rather than all points to all centroids. It is also noted for being less susceptible to initialization problems because it can perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). If a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from Bisecting K-Means can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step, although Bisecting K-Means itself is a valid standalone algorithm.

expert_reference: Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by producing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits. Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points. The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2. This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. A key characteristic of this approach is that it makes local split decisions, meaning it does not jointly optimize all centroids at once; consequently, it can produce different results than standard K-Means with the same target number of clusters. The algorithm is often used to speed up clustering by reducing the number of similarity computations, as it only calculates distances for a subset of points to two centroids at each step rather than all points to all centroids. It is also noted for being less susceptible to initialization problems because it can perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). If a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from Bisecting K-Means can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step, although Bisecting K-Means itself is a valid standalone algorithm.

candidate_draft:
Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm and a straightforward extension of the basic K-means algorithm. It is characterized as a hierarchical sequence of binary splits.

The algorithm follows these steps:
1. Start with one cluster containing all points.
2. Select one existing cluster to split.
3. Apply basic K-Means with K = 2 to that selected cluster to split it into two subclusters.
4. Often, this split is repeated several times with different initializations, and the split with the lowest total SSE is kept.
5. Replace the original cluster with the two new clusters.
6. Repeat this process until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached.

Bisecting K-Means is used to produce better-quality clusterings with lower SSE and is less susceptible to initialization problems than standard K-Means. This is because it only considers two centroids at each step and can perform trial bisections to select the best one. Additionally, it can run significantly faster than regular K-means because, except for the first step, it only computes the distance of a subset of points to the two centroids being considered, thereby reducing the total number of similarities computed.

While Bisecting K-Means is a valid algorithm on its own and useful for taxonomies or broad-to-specific segmentation, it makes local split decisions. Therefore, if the goal is a flat clustering with lower total SSE, the final bisecting centroids can be used as initial centroids for a standard K-Means refinement step, which allows every point to be compared against every final centroid.

expert_reference:
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set. The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity. Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity. This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.

In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix. The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise. When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere. The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.

The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results. By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters. For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks. Additionally, in supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient. In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.

expert_reference:
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set. The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity. Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity. This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.

In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix. The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise. When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere. The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.

The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results. By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters. For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks. Additionally, in supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient. In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.

expert_reference:
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set. The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity. Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity. This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.

In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix. The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise. When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere. The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.

The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results. By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters. For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks. Additionally, in supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient. In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.

expert_reference:
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set. The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity. Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity. This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.

In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix. The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise. When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere. The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.

The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results. By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters. For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks. Additionally, in supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient. In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.

expert_reference:
A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset. This can occur because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect. 

Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible. The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used. For example, Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing, though this can be inaccurate if the frequency of missing values depends on the class label. Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect. In contrast, logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded. 

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on probability; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a surrogate attribute; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value. 

General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation. Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical. Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes). There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.

candidate_draft: Handling missing values in data is crucial for accurate analysis. Missing values can occur in both training and test sets, requiring specific strategies. Decision tree classifiers like C4.5 use probabilistic splits, distributing instances based on attribute probabilities. CART employs surrogate splits, using alternative attributes, while CHAID treats missing values as separate categories. Other methods include imputation, where missing values are replaced with mode or mean, or discarding instances with missing data. Bayesian networks handle missing values by marginalizing their effects, and SVM regression can predict missing values using available data. Each approach has its strengths and is suited to different scenarios.

candidate_system_evidence.text: A decision tree classifier can handle missing attribute values in a number of ways, both in the training and the test sets. When there are missing values in the test set, the classifier must decide which branch to follow if the value of a splitting node attribute is missing for a given test instance. One approach, known as the probabilistic split method, which is employed by the C4.5 decision tree classifier, distributes the data instance to every child of the splitting node according to the probability that the missing attribute has a particular value. In contrast, the CART algorithm uses the surrogate split method, where the instance whose splitting attribute value is missing is assigned to one of the child nodes based on the value of another non-missing surrogate attribute whose splits most resemble the partitions made by the missing attribute. Another approach, known as the separate class method is used by the CHAID algorithm, where the missing value is treated as a separate categorical value distinct from other values of the splitting attribute. Figure 3.18 shows an example of the three different ways for handling missing values in a decision tree classifier. Other strategies for dealing with missing values are based on data preprocessing, where the instance with missing value is either imputed with the mode (for categorical attribute) or mean (for continuous attribute) value or discarded before the classifier is trained.

expert_reference:
A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset. This can occur because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect. 

Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible. The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used. For example, Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing, though this can be inaccurate if the frequency of missing values depends on the class label. Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect. In contrast, logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded. 

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on probability; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a surrogate attribute; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value. 

General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation. Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical. Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes). There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.

The presence of missing values creates three primary problems in data mining: loss of efficiency, complications in handling and analyzing the data, and bias resulting from differences between missing and complete data. These issues can limit the generalizability of research findings. To address these drawbacks, several schemes have been studied, with the most well-known approach being a preprocessing technique formally known as imputation. The literature also identifies simple approaches to missing data, such as the 'do not impute' (DNI) method, which is characterized by its failure to account for the underlying missingness mechanism and its tendency to perform operations blindly. Other strategies include eliminating data objects or attributes with missing values, estimating missing values (such as using nearby ground station data for precipitation), and ignoring missing values during analysis. In the context of decision tree classifiers, missing values can be handled through specific methods like the probabilistic split method used by C4.5, which distributes instances to child nodes based on probability, or the separate class method used by CHAID, which treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value. Preprocessing strategies for classifiers may also involve imputing values with the mode for categorical attributes or the mean for continuous attributes, or discarding instances with missing values before training.

A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset. This can occur because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect. 

Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible. The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used. For example, Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing, though this can be inaccurate if the frequency of missing values depends on the class label. Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect. In contrast, logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded. 

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on probability; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a surrogate attribute; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value. 

General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation. Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical. Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes). There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.

candidate_draft: A missing value occurs when a data object lacks one or more attribute values, or when entire data objects are absent from a dataset. This condition can arise because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are a data quality issue that must be addressed during data analysis, as they can affect the reliability of the analysis if many objects are affected. Different machine learning models handle missing values in distinct ways. For example, Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values in the training set by ignoring the missing values of every attribute while computing conditional probability estimates, and handle missing values in test instances by using only the non-missing attribute values to compute posterior probabilities. However, this approach is inaccurate if the frequency of missing values for a particular attribute value depends on the class label. Bayesian networks can also handle missing values during training and testing by treating the missing attribute as an unobserved node and marginalizing out its effect on the target class. In contrast, logistic regression cannot handle data instances with missing values because it computes posterior probabilities by taking a weighted sum of all attributes; if a test instance has missing values, logistic regression fails to predict its class label. Similarly, artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle instances with missing values in either the training or testing phase. Decision tree classifiers offer several specific strategies for handling missing values in test sets. The probabilistic split method, used by the C4.5 classifier, distributes the data instance to every child of the splitting node according to the probability that the missing attribute has a particular value. The surrogate split method, used by the CART algorithm, assigns the instance to one of the child nodes based on the value of another non-missing surrogate attribute whose splits most resemble the partitions made by the missing attribute. The separate class method, used by the CHAID algorithm, treats the missing value as a separate categorical value distinct from other values of the splitting attribute. Other strategies for dealing with missing values are based on data preprocessing, where the instance with a missing value is either imputed with the mode (for categorical attributes) or mean (for continuous attributes) value, or discarded before the classifier is trained. A simple and effective strategy is to eliminate objects with missing values, which may be expedient if only a few objects are affected, but can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible if many objects have missing values. A related strategy is to eliminate attributes that have missing values, but this should be done with caution because the eliminated attributes may be critical to the analysis. Sometimes missing data can be reliably estimated. For example, in a time series that changes in a reasonably smooth fashion, missing values can be estimated (interpolated) by using the remaining values. In a dataset with many similar data points, the attribute values of the points closest to the point with the missing value are often used to estimate the missing value; for continuous attributes, the average attribute value of the nearest neighbors is used, and for categorical attributes, the most commonly occurring attribute value can be taken. For instance, precipitation measurements for areas not containing a ground station can be estimated using values observed at nearby ground stations. In clustering, if one or both objects of a pair have missing values for some attributes, the similarity can be calculated by using only the attributes that do not have missing values, though the similarity will only be approximate. There is no universal imputation method which performs best for all classifiers.

expert_reference:
A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset. This can occur because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect. 

Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible. The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used. For example, Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing, though this can be inaccurate if the frequency of missing values depends on the class label. Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect. In contrast, logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded. 

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on probability; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a surrogate attribute; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value. 

General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation. Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical. Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes). There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.

Missing values occur when attribute values or entire data objects are absent from a dataset. This can happen because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are considered a data quality issue related to measurement and collection and must be accounted for during data analysis.

Different classifiers handle missing values in varying ways. Naïve Bayes classifiers can handle missing values in the training set by ignoring them when computing conditional probability estimates, and in test instances by using only non-missing attribute values for posterior probabilities. Bayesian networks can handle missing values during both training and testing; for test instances, they perform inference by treating the missing attribute as an unobserved node and marginalizing out its effect on the target class. Decision tree classifiers employ several methods for test sets: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on the probability of the missing attribute's value; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a non-missing surrogate attribute that resembles the missing attribute's partitions; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value.

In contrast, some models cannot handle missing values. Logistic regression and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) cannot handle instances with missing values in the training or testing phase. For logistic regression, training instances with missing values can be discarded, but missing values in a test instance will cause the model to fail to predict the class label.

General strategies for dealing with missing values include data preprocessing steps such as discarding instances or attributes with missing values, or using imputation. Imputation involves estimating missing data, such as using interpolation for smooth time series or using the average (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes) of nearest neighbors. Additionally, similarity calculations for clustering can be performed using only the attributes that are not missing, though this results in an approximate similarity.

candidate_system_evidence.text: A decision tree classifier can handle missing attribute values in a number of ways, both in the training and the test sets. When there are missing values in the test set, the classifier must decide which branch to follow if the value of a splitting node attribute is missing for a given test instance. One approach, known as the probabilistic split method, which is employed by the C4.5 decision tree classifier, distributes the data instance to every child of the splitting node according to the probability that the missing attribute has a particular value. In contrast, the CART algorithm uses the surrogate split method, where the instance whose splitting attribute value is missing is assigned to one of the child nodes based on the value of another non-missing surrogate attribute whose splits most resemble the partitions made by the missing attribute. Another approach, known as the separate class method is used by the CHAID algorithm, where the missing value is treated as a separate categorical value distinct from other values of the splitting attribute. Figure 3.18 shows an example of the three different ways for handling missing values in a decision tree classifier. Other strategies for dealing with missing values are based on data preprocessing, where the instance with missing value is either imputed with the mode (for categorical attribute) or mean (for continuous attribute) value or discarded before the classifier is trained.

In such cases, the missing values can be estimated (interpolated) by using the remaining values. As another example, consider a data set that has many similar data points. In this situation, the attribute values of the points closest to the point with the missing value are often used to estimate the missing value. If the attribute is continuous, then the average attribute value of the nearest neighbors is used; if the attribute is categorical, then the most commonly occurring attribute value can be taken. In data mining, the presence of missing values causes information loss and creates drawbacks for analysis tasks. Because preventing data quality problems is typically not an option, data mining focuses on detecting and correcting these issues or using algorithms that can tolerate poor data quality. Missing values should be taken into account during data analysis, as their presence will likely introduce error or bias unless the pattern of missingness is completely random. An instance with missing values is formally separated into observed values and missing values. Handling missing values is a core part of data preprocessing and data cleaning, distinct from handling wrong or noisy data. While many data mining approaches can be modified to ignore missing values, or to work with them directly, the specific strategies used to resolve them—such as deletion or imputation—belong to sibling concepts. The unit of Missing Value defines the phenomenon and the data state that necessitates these downstream strategies.

candidate_draft: A missingness mechanism describes the underlying process that determines which values in a dataset are missing. Categorizing these mechanisms is a critical step in data preprocessing because the assumptions made about the missingness mechanism and the pattern of missing values directly affect which treatment methods can be correctly applied. The evidence specifically defines the Missing at Random (MAR) mechanism, which is a specific type of missingness mechanism. In the MAR case, the data is partitioned into an observed part (Xobs) and a missing part (Xmis). The defining property of MAR is that the probability of an observation being missing may depend on the observed data (Xobs) but does not depend on the missing data (Xmis). Formally, this is expressed by the condition that the distribution of the missingness indicator B, given the full data X and parameters ζ, is independent of Xmis: P(B|Xobs, Xmis, ζ) = P(B|Xobs, ζ). This implies that for a given set of observed features, the distribution of the remaining features is the same among observed cases as it is among missing cases. The choice of missingness mechanism is also a prerequisite for specific treatments; for instance, multiple imputation (MI) is only applicable when the data follows a Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) or MAR mechanism. Simple preprocessing operations often ignore the missingness mechanism entirely, whereas advanced methods require this categorization to function correctly.

A missingness mechanism refers to the underlying process or distribution that leads to the introduction of missing values (MVs) in a dataset. Categorizing these mechanisms is important because the assumptions made about the missingness mechanism, along with the pattern of missing values, can determine which treatment method can be correctly applied.

One specific mechanism is Missing At Random (MAR). Informally, data is MAR when the probability that an observation is missing may depend on the observed part of the data (Xobs) but not on the missing part (Xmis), where the total data X is composed of X = (Xobs, Xmis). In a MAR mechanism, given specific values for features in Xobs, the distribution of the remaining features is the same for both observed and missing cases.

This mechanism can be represented by a probability model for a matrix B, where B contains variables with values of 1 or 0 indicating whether X elements are observed or missing, respectively. The distribution of B is related to X and unknown parameters ζ, described by P(B|X, ζ). Under the MAR assumption, this distribution does not depend on Xmis, expressed as:

P(B|Xobs, Xmis, ζ) = P(B|Xobs, ζ)

Regarding application, Multiple Imputation (MI) should only be applied when either MCAR or MAR missingness mechanisms hold.

candidate_draft: The missingness mechanism describes the underlying process or pattern that determines how missing values are introduced into a dataset. In real-life data, information is frequently lost in data mining tasks due to the presence of missing values in attributes. When analyzing the missing data mechanism, it is necessary to consider the probability distributions that lie beneath the registration of rectangular data sets, where rows denote different registers, instances, or cases, and columns represent features or variables. A specific example of a missingness mechanism is the Missing at Random (MAR) condition, where, given a particular value or values for a set of observed features, the distribution of the remaining features is the same among the observed cases as it is among the missing cases. The mechanism is a critical factor in data analysis because, unless the pattern with which missing values occurs is completely random, their presence will likely introduce some degree of error and/or bias into the analysis. For certain models of missingness, the only way to obtain an unbiased estimate is to model the missingness mechanism itself. Simple approaches to missing data often do not take the missingness mechanism into account and blindly perform operations, whereas more sophisticated methods formalize these concepts to handle the data appropriately.

expert_reference: The missingness mechanism describes how the probability of a value being missing depends on observed and unobserved data. Under missing at random (MAR), P(B|X_obs,X_mis,ζ) = P(B|X_obs,ζ), so missingness may depend on observed values but not directly on the missing values. Missing completely at random (MCAR) is the more restrictive special case P(B|X_obs,X_mis,ζ) = P(B|ζ), where missingness depends on neither observed nor unobserved data. If MAR does not hold and missingness depends on both observed values and the missing value itself, the source calls the mechanism not missing at random (NMAR) or missing not at random (MNAR).

candidate_draft: The missingness mechanism refers to the underlying process or cause that leads to the introduction of missing values in a dataset. In data mining, information is frequently lost due to the presence of missing values in attributes, which can cause loss of efficiency, complications in handling and analyzing data, and bias resulting from differences between missing and complete data. It is important to categorize these mechanisms because the assumptions made about the missingness mechanism and the pattern of missing values can affect which treatment method could be correctly applied, if any. When thinking about the missing data mechanism, the probability distributions that lie beneath the registration of rectangular data sets should be taken into account, where the rows denote different registers, instances, or cases, and the columns are the features or variables. A common assumption is that the instances are all independent and identically distributed. Some models of missingness present a challenge for the user, as the only way to obtain an unbiased estimate is to model the missingness as well; this is a complex task requiring a model accounting for the missing data to be incorporated into a more complex model used to estimate the missing values. However, even when the missingness model cannot be accounted for, the introduced bias may still be small enough. Simple approaches to missing data, such as not imputing, usually do not take into account the missingness mechanism and blindly perform the operation.

expert_reference:
Imputation is the process of replacing missing values (MVs) in a dataset with estimated values. It is distinguished from deletion strategies, which remove cases containing missing data, and from the classification of missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, NMAR), which describe how data is lost rather than how to fill it. The goal of imputation is to obtain values for non-reference attributes (attributes with missing values) for incomplete objects, using the available reference attributes (attributes with known values).

Imputation methods generally fall into two broad categories: statistical methods and machine learning (ML) methods. Statistical methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Imputation and Expectation-Maximization (EM), model the underlying probability distribution of the data. For example, in a simple coin-flipping scenario where the probability of heads is θ, the maximum likelihood estimate is derived as θ̂ = h/n, where h is the number of heads and n is the total number of flips. More formally, the likelihood is based on a binomial distribution. EM algorithms, often used with Gaussian mixture models, iteratively estimate parameters like the mean (μ) and covariance (Σ) to impute missing values via regression.

Machine learning methods, such as K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI) and Fuzzy K-means Imputation, do not require assuming a specific underlying distribution but still rely on the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption. KMI works by clustering data into K groups, where each cluster is represented by a centroid. The algorithm proceeds in three steps: (1) randomly select K complete data objects as initial centroids; (2) iteratively update the partition to minimize the sum of distances between objects and their assigned centroids until a threshold ε is met or centroids stabilize; and (3) impute missing values for incomplete objects using the cluster information, treating objects in the same cluster as nearest neighbors. Fuzzy K-means imputation extends this by allowing objects to belong to multiple clusters with different membership degrees, calculating imputed values as a weighted sum of cluster centroids based on these memberships. Other approaches include Support Vector Machines Imputation (SVMI) and Hot Deck imputation, which is a historical method used by the Census Bureau.

Evaluating imputation methods is challenging. In unsupervised settings, Mean Squared Error (MSE) or Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) are commonly used to compare imputed values against known true values (by artificially introducing missingness). In supervised settings, such as classification, the goal is to improve classifier accuracy, which is harder to measure directly with MSE/RMSE. Metrics like Wilson’s Noise Ratio may be used to assess the impact of imputation on the learning task.

candidate_draft:
Imputation is a data preprocessing technique used to handle missing values in attributes, a common issue in real-life data mining where information is frequently lost. The goal of imputation is to estimate or fill in these missing values to overcome the drawbacks they produce in data mining tasks. Imputation methods are adapted to the common characteristics of the data analyzed in a specific field, and some procedures from other fields are adapted for use in classification, such as dealing with qualitative data.

There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers. Instead, the choice of imputation method often depends on the type of classifier being used. For example, specific imputation algorithms are recommended for different classification method types, such as the FKMI method for Rule Induction Learning, the EC method for black-box modeling, and the MC method for Lazy Learning models. Imputation methods can be based on statistical approaches, such as sampling from estimated data distributions (including single imputation like Expectation-Maximization and multiple imputation), or on machine learning techniques. Machine learning-based imputation alleviates the need to search for the estimated underlying distribution of the data but is still subject to the Missing at Random (MAR) assumption for correct application. A good imputation method enables the classifier to obtain better accuracy, and imputation methods that fill in missing values generally outperform case deletion or the lack of imputation.

expert_reference:
Imputation is the process of replacing missing values (MVs) in a dataset with estimated values. It is distinguished from deletion strategies, which remove cases containing missing data, and from the classification of missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, NMAR), which describe how data is lost rather than how to fill it. The goal of imputation is to obtain values for non-reference attributes (attributes with missing values) for incomplete objects, using the available reference attributes (attributes with known values).

Imputation methods generally fall into two broad categories: statistical methods and machine learning (ML) methods. Statistical methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Imputation and Expectation-Maximization (EM), model the underlying probability distribution of the data. For example, in a simple coin-flipping scenario where the probability of heads is θ, the maximum likelihood estimate is derived as θ̂ = h/n, where h is the number of heads and n is the total number of flips. More formally, the likelihood is based on a binomial distribution. EM algorithms, often used with Gaussian mixture models, iteratively estimate parameters like the mean (μ) and covariance (Σ) to impute missing values via regression.

Machine learning methods, such as K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI) and Fuzzy K-means Imputation, do not require assuming a specific underlying distribution but still rely on the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption. KMI works by clustering data into K groups, where each cluster is represented by a centroid. The algorithm proceeds in three steps: (1) randomly select K complete data objects as initial centroids; (2) iteratively update the partition to minimize the sum of distances between objects and their assigned centroids until a threshold ε is met or centroids stabilize; and (3) impute missing values for incomplete objects using the cluster information, treating objects in the same cluster as nearest neighbors. Fuzzy K-means imputation extends this by allowing objects to belong to multiple clusters with different membership degrees, calculating imputed values as a weighted sum of cluster centroids based on these memberships. Other approaches include Support Vector Machines Imputation (SVMI) and Hot Deck imputation, which is a historical method used by the Census Bureau.

Evaluating imputation methods is challenging. In unsupervised settings, Mean Squared Error (MSE) or Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) are commonly used to compare imputed values against known true values (by artificially introducing missingness). In supervised settings, such as classification, the goal is to improve classifier accuracy, which is harder to measure directly with MSE/RMSE. Metrics like Wilson’s Noise Ratio may be used to assess the impact of imputation on the learning task.

candidate_draft:
Imputation is the process of replacing missing values (MVs) in a dataset with estimated values. It is distinguished from deletion strategies, which remove cases or attributes, and from the classification of missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, NMAR), which describe how data is lost. The goal of imputation is to obtain values for non-reference attributes (attributes with missing data) for incomplete objects, using the available reference attributes. 

Imputation methods can be broadly categorized into statistical and machine learning approaches. Statistical methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Imputation, model the underlying probability distribution of the data. For example, in a simple binomial case where the probability of heads is θ, the maximum likelihood estimate is derived as θ̂ = h/n, where h is the number of heads and n is the total number of flips. More formally, the likelihood is obtained from a binomial distribution: P(θ) = C(n,h) * θ^h * (1-θ)^(n-h). The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is another statistical approach that assumes the data follows a probability distribution, such as a multivariate Gaussian, and iteratively revises estimates of the mean and covariance to impute missing values using conditional expectations.

Machine learning-based imputation methods, such as K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI) and Fuzzy K-means Clustering Imputation, do not require assuming a specific underlying distribution. KMI divides the dataset into K clusters and uses the cluster centroids to impute missing values. The algorithm involves three processes: (1) randomly selecting K complete data objects as centroids, (2) iteratively modifying the partition to reduce the sum of distances between objects and their cluster centroids until a threshold is met, and (3) filling in non-reference attributes for incomplete objects based on the cluster information. In Fuzzy K-means, each data object belongs to all K clusters with different membership degrees, and the imputed value for a non-reference attribute j is calculated as the sum of the membership degree of the object in each cluster multiplied by the centroid value for that attribute: x_{i,j} = Σ_{k=1}^{K} U(x_i, ν_k) * ν_{k,j}. 

The choice of imputation method depends on the context. In unsupervised settings, methods that generate values close to the true unknown values are preferred, often evaluated using Mean Square Error (MSE) or Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). In supervised settings, such as classification, a good imputation method enables the classifier to obtain better accuracy, which is harder to measure directly. The use of machine learning methods for imputation alleviates the need to search for the estimated underlying distribution of the data, but they are still subject to the MAR (Missing At Random) assumption to be correctly applied.
